phonemes.desc: Initial alpha with acute: a high-pitched, open [a].
Delta followed by long omega [oː], the stressed length of the name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-doh-nis' — pitch falls on the first syllable, and the middle vowel is long.

kin.label: Semitic

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ἄδωνις — the Semitic title fitted with Greek inflection; the goddess who loved him kept her Semitic memory in the title ʾādōn

pronunciation.note: The Greek form Ἄδωνις reproduces the Semitic title ʾādōn ('lord') with Greek inflection. The restoration Ádōnis preserves both the acute stress and the long omega.

domains.title: Lord of Beauty and Brief Return
domains.subtitle: Desire, Vegetation, and the Cycle of Death and Renewal
domains.lead: Ádōnis is the beautiful youth whom love and death divide. Born from the grief of Myrrha and the myrrh tree, desired by Aphrodítē and Persephonē alike, he embodies the fragile glory of spring: flowers that bloom brilliantly and die young. His cult spread across the Greek East as a women's rite of lament and rebirth.

cards.name: Beauty and Desire
cards.desc: A youth of such beauty that the goddess of love herself cannot leave him.

cards.name: Vegetation and Renewal
cards.desc: The anemone and the myrrh tree mark his blood and birth; his death is the death of the green year.

cards.name: Women's Lament
cards.desc: The Adṓnia was a rite of mourning women, planting gardens that withered to enact grief.

cards.name: Hunter Hunted
cards.desc: A boar, the animal of Aphrodítē's anger or of his own hubris, tears him open.

symbols.name: Anemone
symbols.meaning: The flower that sprang from Ádōnis's blood, red and short-lived

symbols.name: Myrrh tree
symbols.meaning: His mother Myrrha's metamorphosis; the tree from whose bark he was born

symbols.name: Boar
symbols.meaning: The animal that killed him in the hunt

symbols.name: Hunter's gear
symbols.meaning: Spear and nets; the masculine pursuit that leads to his death

mythology.lead: Ádōnis's myth turns on beauty that cannot be kept. He is desired, born, killed, and divided — a story the Greeks borrowed from the dying-god cults of the Near East and made their own, and a women's rite of lament that gives rare direct voice to female grief in the classical city.

myths.title: The Myrrh Tree Splits
myths.text: Myrrha, daughter of King Kinyras of Cyprus — or of Assyria, in the older eastern versions — conceived a hopeless passion for her own father. Her nurse smuggled her into the royal bed on a night when the king's wife was away at a festival of Demeter; when Kinyras discovered the truth by lamplight he reached for his sword, and the gods transformed the fleeing girl into a myrrh tree (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.4; Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.298–502). Ten months later the bark split and the infant Adonis was born — Ovid's loveliest detail has the tree tear 'like a girl's body opening in childbirth'. The tale makes his beauty the fruit of transgression: he is born where the boundary of the family was crossed, and his whole career will be spent on boundaries — between women and men, love and death, the earth and the underworld.

myths.title: Divided Between Two Queens
myths.text: Aphrodite hid the infant in a chest and entrusted him to Persephone, queen of the dead — but Persephone opened the chest, looked, and refused to give him back. Zeus judged between the goddesses: Adonis would spend a third of the year with Persephone below, a third with Aphrodite above, and a third as he chose — and he chose Aphrodite, for love of her beauty and the living world (Apollodorus 3.14.4). Sappho preserves the women's lament for the dying season — 'tender Adonis is dying, Cyprian; what shall we do?' (fr. 140a) — and a variant has the division decided by lots weighed on a scale, Aphrodite cheating with her girdle to tip the outcome. The myth is transparent seasonal allegory: the year itself divided between the queen of life and the queen of death. Its honesty is the point — desire and mortality get exactly equal terms.

myths.title: The Boar on the Mountain
myths.text: Despite Aphrodite's warnings, Adonis hunted a wild boar. The beast gored him in the thigh — some say the boar was Aphrodite's own anger made flesh, or the jealous Ares in animal shape; others blame the youth's recklessness, for he hunted what his protector feared (Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.705–739). He died in Aphrodite's arms, and where his blood struck the earth the anemone sprang up — red, wind-shaken, and short-lived, a flower that nods in the slightest breeze, as Ovid says, 'because it grew from tears'. Persephone received him below, and the goddess's grief became the template for the women's rite. The death of the beautiful hunter is one of antiquity's most retold scenes precisely because it refuses consolation: not resurrection, not apotheosis — only a flower, and a goddess weeping over it every year.

myths.title: The Gardens of Adonis
myths.text: The Adonia was the women's festival of Adonis, attested across the Greek world: at Athens the rooftop ritual mocked by Aristophanes (Lysistrata 387–398); at Alexandria the grand procession of a wax effigy that Theocritus sets in the mouths of two Syracusan women (Idyll 15); and in Syria the temple rites at Byblos that Lucian describes, where the god's death is mourned and his resurrection celebrated (On the Syrian Goddess 6). Its signature rite was the 'gardens of Adonis': lettuces, fennel, and quick-sprouting herbs planted in shallow trays, forced into brief green life, then carried to the rooftops to wither in the sun — miniature lives enacted and lost within days. Plato's Socrates borrows the image (Phaedrus 276b) to dismiss writing itself: the written word, he says, is like a garden of Adonis — pretty, rootless, dead quickly. The cult gives rare direct evidence of women's religious life in the classical city.

lore.syncretism: Ádōnis is transparently the Greek adaptation of the Semitic Tammuz (Sumerian Dumuzi), the dying-and-rising vegetation god mourned by women in Mesopotamia and the Levant. The name itself comes from the Canaanite/Phoenician ʾādōn, 'lord'. In Roman poetry he becomes a byword for youthful male beauty — Venus and Adonis is a staple of Ovid and later painters, and Shakespeare's poem and Titian's canvases carry the pair into the modern canon. The figure also overlaps with Near Eastern dying-god typologies studied by Frazer, though modern scholars resist collapsing every vegetation deity into a single pattern.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ádōnis survives in the anemone, in the word 'Adonis' applied to handsome young men, and in the long Western tradition of Venus and Adonis from Ovid to Shakespeare to Titian. His cult is one of the clearest cases of religious borrowing across the Aegean and Levant, and the Adṓnia gives rare evidence for women's religious practice in classical Greece. In modern wellness and beauty branding, his name still signals youth, desire, and the fleeting bloom of physical perfection.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ádōnis is the god of what cannot last. Every spring his myth asks: why do the most beautiful things die first? The answer is not theological; it is seasonal. He is the flower, the harvest, the young lover, the grief that returns every year. To worship Ádōnis is to consent to love something you will lose.

Yet the loss is not final. The anemone returns. The women plant new gardens. The rite enacts not despair but cyclical hope — beauty dies, beauty returns, and the lament itself becomes the vessel of return. Ádōnis is therefore a god not of endings but of the interval between endings, the green moment before the heat of summer takes it away.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is attested in Greek as Ἄδωνις. The initial alpha carries an acute, and the omega is long. PUNICODEX restores these features as Ádōnis; the Semitic original ʾādōn is not registrable in the .com IDN table and is preserved here as scholarly annotation.
lore.archaeology: Adonis has left no excavated sanctuary in the Greek world — the Adonia were rooftop and garden rites that leave no foundations — but his cult has a concrete Levantine landscape. At Afqa in the mountains above Byblos, a great grotto and spring burst from the cliff: the source of the river the Greeks called Adonis, the modern Nahr Ibrahim, whose floodwaters stained red with mountain clay were read as the god's annual blood (Lucian, On the Syrian Goddess 6). Roman remains at the site include temple platforms and aqueduct lines of the sanctuary of Venus and Adonis. Below, the harbours of Byblos — whose royal house claimed kinship with Adonis's father Kinyras — anchor the myth to one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on earth.
